name: Summer station
note: After Trevor Kincaid scouted the islands in 1903, UW zoologists and botanists brought small groups of teachers and students to Friday Harbor each summer from 1904. They camped in tents beside a borrowed cabin and later worked out of a waterfront cannery. There were no permanent buildings, and at first no formal classes; the seasons were spent collecting and dredging, and they won the town's backing for a permanent laboratory.

name: Puget Sound Marine Station
note: In 1909 the station got land of its own, given by Andrew Newhall on the Friday Harbor waterfront, and a new name that presented it as a regional laboratory shared by several colleges. Under directors Trevor Kincaid and then T. C. Frye it built its first laboratory over the water, started a research series, and drew summer students and scientists from across the country, most of whom lived in tents. By 1916 the steep, polluted site was clearly too small, and the university turned to the Point Caution military reserve.

name: Puget Sound Biological Station
note: Renamed during World War I, the Puget Sound Biological Station won the 484-acre Point Caution reserve from Congress in 1921 and moved there in 1924, putting up laboratories that are still in use. Under Frye it stayed mainly a summer school for teachers and visiting biologists, but the sessions grew longer and larger and its publications made it known abroad. In 1923 the state also declared the surrounding waters a marine biological preserve.

name: UW Oceanographic Laboratories
note: With Rockefeller Foundation money, chemist Thomas G. Thompson made the station the field branch of UW's new Oceanographic Laboratories, with its own research ship, the Catalyst. During World War II the Coast Guard took over the campus, and a 1950 budget cut nearly closed it. A 1952 review set the course toward a year-round marine biology station, and by 1956 it had separated from oceanography in Seattle.

name: Friday Harbor Laboratories
note: As Friday Harbor Laboratories, the station became a year-round center for marine biology, with NSF-funded buildings, spring and fall programs for undergraduates, and more than 1,500 acres of preserves. Work begun here, from the jellyfish proteins behind a 2008 Nobel Prize to the rescue of the sunflower sea star, has had effects well beyond the islands. Recent years have brought new research centers, closer ties with Coast Salish peoples, a pandemic and tight budgets.
